input: 3 seconds of mono audio at 48 kHz (144,000 samples)
output: a raw score (logit) for each species; the page turns it into a score from 0 to 1 with a sigmoid
preprocessing: Each 3-second window has its mean removed and is scaled so that its loudest sample is 0.9, with at most +40 dB of gain (faint-call normalisation). The page does the same before the recogniser runs.

base.name: BirdNET GLOBAL 6K V2.4
base.authors: Stefan Kahl, Connor M. Wood, Maximilian Eibl and Holger Klinck
base.citation: Kahl, S., Wood, C. M., Eibl, M., & Klinck, H. (2021). BirdNET: A deep learning solution for avian diversity monitoring. Ecological Informatics 61, 101236.

training.method: BirdNET V2.4 is kept as it is; a new two-layer classifier on its embeddings was trained with BirdNET-Analyzer, with a background class for noise alone.
training.augmentation: Training copies were mixed with wind (recorded and synthetic), crowd chatter, bush ambience and people sounds at -5 to 20 dB, and some were made faint. Night recordings got one and a half times as many copies.

thresholds.note: These are the sigmoid of raw scores 0.5 and 0.25, the cut-offs used in testing.

test.note: 58 held-out clips from 10 species, clean and mixed with noise that was never used in training. A clip's score is its best 3-second window. Few clips a species, so one clip moves a species' score a lot.
